subproblems.title: Derivative of the weighted radial cutoff integral s -> int phi(|x - y|/s) f(x) dmu(x) (accepted declaration, reused)
subproblems.statement: Let n, l be natural numbers, E := R^{n+l} (Euclidean space), mu a measure on E, y in E, f : E -> R, phi : R -> R and S, T, t real numbers. Write r(x) := |x - y|, B_S(y) for the closed ball of radius S about y, and phi' := deriv phi. Assume: f is mu-integrable on B_S(y); phi is C^1; T > 0; phi(u) = 0 for every u >= T; t > 0; and T t < S. Then the function s -> integral_E phi(r(x)/s) f(x) dmu(x) has derivative -(integral_E (r(x)/t) phi'(r(x)/t) f(x) dmu(x))/t at s = t. Integrals are Bochner integrals, and division follows Lean's convention x/0 = 0.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Amb n ℓ)) (y : Amb n ℓ) (f : Amb n ℓ → ℝ) (φ : ℝ → ℝ) (S T t : ℝ), IntegrableOn f (closedBall y S) μ → ContDiff ℝ 1 φ → 0 < T → (∀ u : ℝ, T ≤ u → φ u = 0) → 0 < t → T * t < S → HasDerivAt (fun s => ∫ x, φ (‖x - y‖ / s) * f x ∂μ) (-(∫ x, ‖x - y‖ / t * deriv φ (‖x - y‖ / t) * f x ∂μ) / t) t
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: steps 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 of the supplied proof of ted_lpm_fcm_cutoff_mass_hasDerivAt (Simon, Ch. 4, 4.3: differentiation of the cutoff mass in the scale), carried out with the weight f. The selected statement's part (c) is the case f = 1. This is the comparator-accepted declaration allard52_am_cc_cutoff_integral_hasDerivAt, reused with its identical frozen type.

Notation: r(x) := |x - y|, phi' := deriv phi, B := B_S(y) the closed ball, nu := mu restricted to B, R := S/T.

1. Properties of phi.
 (a) phi is C^1. Hence phi and phi' are continuous (ContDiff.continuous, ContDiff.continuous_deriv_one), and phi has derivative phi'(u) at every u (ContDiff.differentiable, since 1 != 0).
 (b) phi'(u) = 0 for u > T. The open set (T, infinity) is a neighbourhood of u, and phi = 0 on it because every v there satisfies T <= v. So phi agrees near u with the zero function, and phi'(u) = 0 (Filter.EventuallyEq.deriv_eq, deriv_const).
 (c) Bounds. The continuous functions phi and u -> u phi'(u) are bounded on the compact interval [0, T] (IsCompact.exists_bound_of_continuousOn): |phi(u)| <= K0 and |u phi'(u)| <= C0 there. Put K := max(K0, 0) and C := max(C0, 0); in particular C >= 0. For u > T, phi(u) = 0 by hypothesis and u phi'(u) = 0 by (b). Hence |phi(u)| <= K and |u phi'(u)| <= C for every u >= 0.

2. Localisation. Since T > 0, for every real s we have s < R iff T s < S. In particular t < R. Let 0 < s < R and let x lie outside B. Then r(x) > S > T s, so r(x)/s > T. Hence phi(r(x)/s) = 0 by hypothesis and phi'(r(x)/s) = 0 by 1(b).

3. Pointwise derivative. Fix a real r and s != 0. The map u -> r/u = r u^{-1} has derivative r(-(s^2)^{-1}) = -r/s^2 at s (hasDerivAt_inv). By the chain rule and 1(a), u -> phi(r/u) has derivative phi'(r/s)(-r/s^2) = -((r/s) phi'(r/s))/s at s.

4. Integrability and measurability for nu.
 - Since f is mu-integrable on B, f is nu-integrable. Hence f is nu-a.e. strongly measurable and |f| is nu-integrable.
 - Put F(s, x) := phi(r(x)/s) f(x) and F'(s, x) := -((r(x)/s) phi'(r(x)/s))/s * f(x).
 - For each s, x -> phi(r(x)/s) is continuous on E as a composition of continuous maps. So F(s, .) is nu-a.e. strongly measurable, as the product of a continuous function and an a.e. strongly measurable one.
 - Likewise F'(t, .) is nu-a.e. strongly measurable, since x -> -((r(x)/t) phi'(r(x)/t))/t is continuous by 1(a).
 - F(t, .) is nu-integrable: r(x)/t >= 0, so |F(t, x)| <= K |f(x)| by 1(c), and K |f| is nu-integrable (Integrable.mono').

5. Differentiation under the integral sign for nu. Let N := (t/2, R). It is an open interval containing t (because t/2 < t < R), hence a neighbourhood of t. Use the bound b(x) := (2C/t)|f(x)|, which is nu-integrable.
 - Domination. Let x be arbitrary and s in N. Then s > t/2 > 0 and r(x)/s >= 0, so by 1(c), |F'(s, x)| = (|(r(x)/s) phi'(r(x)/s)|/s) |f(x)| <= (C/s)|f(x)| <= (2C/t)|f(x)| = b(x). This uses C >= 0 and 1/s < 2/t.
 - Differentiability. Let x be arbitrary and s in N. Then s != 0, so by step 3, multiplied by the constant f(x), the map u -> F(u, x) has derivative F'(s, x) at s.
 Step 4 gives the remaining hypotheses: measurability of F(s, .) for every s, integrability of F(t, .), and measurability of F'(t, .). The theorem on differentiation under the integral sign (hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_deriv_le, with the neighbourhood N and the bound b) then shows that s -> integral F(s, x) dnu(x) has derivative integral F'(t, x) dnu(x) at t.

6. Back to mu.
 - For 0 < s < R, F(s, .) vanishes outside B by step 2. Hence integral F(s, x) dmu = integral over B of F(s, x) dmu = integral F(s, x) dnu (setIntegral_eq_integral_of_forall_compl_eq_zero, which needs no integrability).
 - (0, R) is an open neighbourhood of t, so s -> integral F(s, x) dmu and s -> integral F(s, x) dnu agree near t. The first therefore also has derivative integral F'(t, x) dnu at t (HasDerivAt.congr_of_eventuallyEq).
 - Write G(x) := (r(x)/t) phi'(r(x)/t) f(x). Pointwise F'(t, x) = -G(x)/t, so integral F'(t, x) dnu = -(integral G dnu)/t (integral_neg, integral_div; these identities hold for every function).
 - G vanishes outside B by step 2 with s = t, so integral G dnu = integral G dmu.
 Therefore s -> integral phi(r(x)/s) f(x) dmu(x) has derivative -(integral (r(x)/t) phi'(r(x)/t) f(x) dmu(x))/t at t.
proof_key_steps: phi and phi' are continuous, phi' = 0 on (T, infinity), and |phi(u)| <= K, |u phi'(u)| <= C with C >= 0 for all u >= 0 (compactness of [0, T]).
For 0 < s < S/T, the integrands phi(r/s) f and (r/s) phi'(r/s) f vanish off B_S(y), because r/s > T there.
For s != 0, the derivative of u -> phi(r/u) at s is -((r/s) phi'(r/s))/s (chain rule with hasDerivAt_inv).
For nu = mu restricted to B_S(y): F(s,.) is measurable, F(t,.) is integrable (bound K|f|), and F'(s,.) is dominated by (2C/t)|f| for s in (t/2, S/T).
hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_deriv_le gives the derivative of the nu-integral at t.

The mu- and nu-integrals agree on (0, S/T). Transfer the derivative (HasDerivAt.congr_of_eventuallyEq) and rewrite its value as -(int (r/t) phi'(r/t) f dmu)/t (integral_neg, integral_div, vanishing off the ball).

subproblems.title: Integrability of a continuous radial profile g(|x - y|/t) that vanishes beyond T
subproblems.statement: Let n, l be natural numbers, E := R^{n+l} (Euclidean space), mu a measure on E, y in E, g : R -> R and S, T, t real numbers. Write B_S(y) for the closed ball of radius S about y. Assume: mu(B_S(y)) < infinity; g is continuous; g(u) = 0 for every u > T; t > 0; and T t < S. Then the real function x -> g(|x - y|/t) is mu-integrable on E.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Amb n ℓ)) (y : Amb n ℓ) (g : ℝ → ℝ) (S T t : ℝ), μ (closedBall y S) < ⊤ → Continuous g → (∀ u : ℝ, T < u → g u = 0) → 0 < t → T * t < S → Integrable (fun x => g (‖x - y‖ / t)) μ
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: steps 1(c), 2 and 3 of the supplied proof of ted_lpm_fcm_cutoff_mass_hasDerivAt (the integrability parts (a) and (b)), stated for an arbitrary continuous radial profile g. Part (a) is the case g = phi; part (b) is the case g(u) = u phi'(u).

Notation: B := B_S(y) the closed ball, h(x) := g(|x - y|/t).

1. A bound for g on [0, infinity). g is continuous, hence bounded on the compact interval [0, T], which is empty if T < 0 (IsCompact.exists_bound_of_continuousOn). So there is K0 with |g(u)| <= K0 for all u in [0, T]. Put K := max(K0, 0).
 - If 0 <= u <= T, then |g(u)| <= K0 <= K.
 - If u > T, then g(u) = 0 by hypothesis, so |g(u)| = 0 <= K.
 Hence |g(u)| <= K for every u >= 0.

2. Measurability. h is continuous on E, as the composition of the continuous maps x -> |x - y|, division by the constant t, and g. A continuous real function on E is a.e. strongly measurable for every measure (E carries its Borel sigma-algebra), in particular for mu restricted to B.

3. Uniform bound. For every x in E, |x - y|/t >= 0 because t > 0. So |h(x)| <= K by step 1.

4. Integrability on B. B has finite mu-measure by hypothesis. By steps 2 and 3, h is a.e. strongly measurable for mu restricted to B and bounded by K there. Hence h is integrable on B (IntegrableOn.of_bound).

5. Vanishing off B. Let x lie outside B. Then |x - y| > S, and S > T t by hypothesis, so |x - y| > T t. Dividing by t > 0 gives |x - y|/t > T, hence h(x) = g(|x - y|/t) = 0.

6. Conclusion. h is integrable on B and vanishes at every point outside B, so h is mu-integrable (IntegrableOn.integrable_of_forall_notMem_eq_zero).
proof_key_steps: |g(u)| <= K for all u >= 0, by compactness of [0, T] and g = 0 on (T, infinity).
x -> g(|x - y|/t) is continuous, hence a.e. strongly measurable, and it is bounded by K everywhere because |x - y|/t >= 0.
It is integrable on B_S(y), which has finite mu-measure (IntegrableOn.of_bound).
It vanishes outside B_S(y), because there |x - y| > S > T t gives |x - y|/t > T.
Being integrable on B_S(y) and zero outside it, the function is mu-integrable (IntegrableOn.integrable_of_forall_notMem_eq_zero).
